nodes.description: Voelke opens against the frequently held thesis (Opstelten's special study; Pohlenz's claim that the Greeks recognised no volitional function distinct from the intellectual ones) that the philosophical notion of will originates in the Roman genius and the Christian message and owes nothing to Greek thought. Rather than choosing within the alternative 'voluntarism vs intellectualism', an effort of precision applied to Stoic rationalism should lead us to reject the alternative itself, 'en nous montrant que dans cette doctrine la raison est volonté' — by showing that in this doctrine reason is will. The book pursues this in two stages: the fundamental conceptions (largely Chrysippus' work) and the post-Chrysippean developments (Panaetius, Posidonius, Marcus Aurelius; then Epictetus; finally Seneca).
nodes.label: Voelke: in Stoic rationalism reason itself is will — against the thesis that Greek thought ignored the will

nodes.description: Voelke's concluding synthesis: the activity of the soul's ruling part is exercised through operative 'functions' with no reality other than their exercise. Two of them are voluntary — in Stoic terms 'in our power': judgement and tendency (tendance, hormē). Judgement is the soul's assent subscribing to its own movement towards the true or the good (in Cicero's Latin transposition this assent is qualified as voluntary); tendency can take the form of the rational desire of the good, for which Cicero adopted the term voluntas. A closer examination reveals a relation of reciprocity: judgement determines the ends towards which we tend, but tendency furnishes judgement the norms needed for its exercise; only by abstraction are they separated, since all conduct binds them in a single act. Both are therefore derived forms of a primordial will which is tension, force, effort upon itself.
nodes.label: Voelke: judgement (assent) and tendency are the two volitional functions 'in our power', united by reciprocity

nodes.description: Against philosophers who define will by effort against a resisting object (a conception implying exteriority, as in Maine de Biran), Voelke argues that in the old Stoa effort in its primordial form supposes no exteriority of agent to patient: it is the tension of a corporeal pneuma that moves itself and thereby maintains its individual unity. Its action opposes no antagonistic force but an internal inertia which is only a lack of tension; when tension is at its highest degree, every trace of inertia disappears and action is exercised without effort — the case of divine action (Cicero, Nat. Deor. III 39, 92) and, analogously, of the sage, whose tension is a triumphant force assuring his life its unimpeded course. Voelke links this to the Cynic heritage: the Stoic notion of tension takes up and deepens the Cynic notion of effort (ponos), Cleanthes making Heracles' universal tension the force of nature itself.
nodes.label: Voelke: the primordial Stoic will is immanent tension (tonos) of the pneuma, not effort against resistance

nodes.description: Chapter VI, 'Le consentement au Destin'. Only the willing that consents to Destiny is safe from failure and can greet every event as the realisation of its own aspiration; its best expression is Cleanthes' prayer (ap. Epictetus, Man. 53 = SVF I, 527). Consent to Destiny realises the perfect accord of the soul's functions, each carried to its highest power: 'acte volontaire par excellence', proper to the rational being, uniting the diverse forms of willing previously distinguished. It requires that the universe be first understood as a cosmos ordered by providence — there is no genuine consent without intelligence — and it is not mere passive resignation to the inevitable but an act of assent by which man subscribes to the truth and perfection of the Whole; by this act we accede to freedom (Seneca, Vit. beat. 15, 7: Deo parere libertas est). It is also cooperation, an incessant effort to eliminate hostility to the cosmic order, and it mobilises anticipation of the future (the praemeditatio recommended since Posidonius) so as to master events by representing them in advance.
nodes.label: Voelke: consent to Destiny is the voluntary act par excellence, not passive resignation

nodes.description: It does not suffice to characterise Stoic consent to Destiny psychologically; seized in its foundation it reveals the very structure of the universe. That foundation is the universal sympathy that assures the unity of the cosmos: sympathy is 'con-spiration' (sympnoia) and 'syntonie' (syntonia), the internal harmony of a cosmos all of whose parts are moved by the tension of a single divine breath. Our souls sympathise with the Whole, united to God as parts; man alone can become conscious of this communication and, if he can deny it, he can also consciously re-establish it — to re-unite himself to the Whole and 'reprendre sa place de partie' (Marcus Aurelius VIII, 34). Consent, first manifest as assent and tendency, is thus more profoundly an effort to realise the syntonia, the accord between the tension of the individual soul and that of the divine pneuma. Voelke notes (following K. Reinhardt) that the doctrine of universal sympathy holds a particularly large place among imperial Stoics, doubtless under Posidonius' influence, but its elements are already ancient Stoic.
nodes.label: Voelke: universal sympathy is the ontological foundation of consent to Destiny

nodes.description: Chapter VII, 'La volonté de la Nature'. Diverse Stoic texts present nature as an agent exercising voluntary activity: identified with the omnipresent logos, Destiny and Providence, nature is a self-moving generative fire proceeding methodically (Galen, Defin. med. 95 = SVF II, 1133), and in the exposé following Zeno's definition the nature of the world possesses all the movements, tendencies and inclinations of will — hormai — with corresponding actions (Cicero, Nat. Deor. II 22, 58 = SVF I, 172). Unlike Aristotle's nature, which 'wants' but cannot move itself and depends on a transcendent first mover, Stoic nature is a self-moving rational power. The idea of a will of nature appears most clearly in the imperial period: Epictetus exhorts us to become conscious of the boulēma tēs physeōs; Seneca's Naturales Quaestiones treat the laws of universal nature as voluntary decrees, and natural facts as expressions of a will tending to man's moral edification; Marcus Aurelius distinguishes the will of common nature from that of man's own nature and defines obedience to nature under both aspects. Since to identify tension with a primordial form of will is to make nature itself will, the Stoics' talk of a 'volonté de la nature' is no abuse of language.
nodes.label: Voelke: Stoic nature itself wills — the 'volonté de la nature' is clearest in the imperial Stoa

nodes.description: Voelke's reading of the Stoic reconciliation of freedom and fate: every tension-produced nature is a cause 'parfaite en elle-même' (perfecta et principalis, Cicero, De Fato 18, 41), acting by its own virtue while external conditions remain merely auxiliary and proximate causes. When the perfect cause is in us, our action is 'in our power', which for the Stoics means it is free: the assent given to a representation is free, even though conditioned by an impression of external origin, because in it the soul's own force and nature express themselves (suapte vi et natura, De Fato 19, 43) — not a separate faculty, but reason acting as cause perfect in itself. Our will thus identifies with our nature insofar as nature determines itself according to its own force and affirms or denies its rational essence. Consequently this conception absolutely excludes a willing freed from the cosmic order — whether surging up as an arbitrary caprice without cause, in the manner of the Epicurean clinamen, or breaking the chain of events by inserting itself without necessity, in the manner of Carneades' fortuitous cause (Cicero, De Fato 10, 22-11, 25).
nodes.label: Voelke: assent is free because its perfect and principal cause is in us — a will identical with our rational nature

nodes.description: Second-part thesis: from Panaetius on, Stoic anthropology undergoes modifications that bear on the conception of will. The psychological monism which had reached its most achieved form with Chrysippus gives way to a more or less marked dualism; certain functions of the soul stand out and concentrate in themselves powers the old Stoa had attributed to the whole ruling part. In Posidonius and Marcus Aurelius the tendencies — or some of them — cease to be rational powers and become foreign forces which reason must hold in obedience while keeping itself pure of contamination; the élan of tendency and the judgement of reason can then no longer be regarded as two manifestations of one fundamental will, and tendency figures as exterior to volition. In Marcus Aurelius volition identifies itself with the movement of a spirit separate from the soul, while tendency, attached to the soul, is considered involuntary — a thesis prefiguring Plotinus, for whom the only free activity 'in our power' is that of the spirit (Plotinus VI 8, 3 and 8, 6).
nodes.label: Voelke: from Panaetius onward, psychological dualism detaches tendency from the will of reason

nodes.description: Seneca's reflections on the will do not form a systematically elaborated doctrine, but he tends to make will the determining element of morality: militant, it is the artisan of all progress; triumphant, the living realisation of the good; perverted, the essence of evil. In his stress on the will Seneca is often close to Augustine: both feel profoundly the inner tearing of the soul and evoke it in almost identical terms — the divided soul does not will 'totally' and floats between diverse volitions (Seneca, Ep. 20, 6 and 35, 4; Augustine, Conf. VIII 9, 21 and 10, 22-23). But for Seneca the will realises its unity by progressing towards virtue, whereas for Augustine the tearing is overcome only if the will returns to God, since the evil it suffers is a consequence of Adam's sin. Augustine, noting that ordinary usage does not respect the Stoic distinction between the eupathic terms ('to will') and the passional ones ('to desire'), substitutes for the sage/fool opposition the more fundamental opposition between good and bad will: willing and desiring, the good and the wicked both do; the movements are good or bad according as the will is right or perverse (Civ. Dei XIV, 6 and 8). Where Seneca is convinced nature gave us the force to straighten a perverted will, for the theologian of grace only God can redress and free the enslaved will.
nodes.label: Voelke: Seneca makes will the determining element of morality and anticipates Augustine's divided will

nodes.description: Against critics who write as though the Stoics taught belief in fate in order to attain tranquility (von Fritz's summation is quoted), Brennan argues the putative ethical motivation for Stoic determinism fails twice. First, Epictetus holds it is psychologically impossible to use beliefs about Zeus and fate to alter our beliefs about good and bad: piety presupposes, and cannot produce, the conviction that externals are not goods (Diss. 1.22.13-16, 2.22.15-17, 1.27.12-14) — the ethical point that only virtue is good must be secured first. Second, what happens is not good but indifferent, and any other arrangement Zeus provided would be equally indifferent; the world is the most rational, not the best, of all possible worlds, so reflections on providence either cannot console or are not needed. The theory of fate is so closely connected to Stoic logic, physics and theology that it would be a distortion to say it was adopted to score an ethical point; indeed (opening of ch. 17) the doctrine of fate has no drastic consequences for Stoic ethics, and thinking it crucial to Stoic ethics is a mistake to be set right.
nodes.label: Brennan: the Stoics did not adopt determinism for ethical or consolatory reasons

nodes.description: On the 'Fabius Argument' (Cicero, De Fato 12-15): if divinatory theorems are true conditionals linking a necessary past fact to a prediction, whatever conflicts with them becomes impossible, so nothing predicted is 'up to us'. Chrysippus' response — recasting the theorems as negated conjunctions ('not both: born at the rising of Sirius, and dies at sea'), which assert no conflict — succeeds in defusing the argument as stated, since it denies that divination needs conditionals expressing necessary connections; Cicero's mockery about teaching the Chaldeans their grammar misses this solid point. But Brennan adds that the response does not settle the issue: showing that divinatory theorems do not express necessary connections does not show that there are no necessary connections between past and future; the science may depend for its coherence on an underlying causal network, unless causes can be split from necessitation.
nodes.label: Brennan: Chrysippus' negated-conjunction reply defuses the divination argument but leaves the necessity question open

nodes.description: Reconstruction of the cylinder-and-cone response (Cicero, De Fato 40-43): Chrysippus does not claim the agent could have received the same impression and not assented; given the shove and the shape, the rolling is completely determined, and the assent is caused, determined and fated. What the analogy shows is that the impression by itself is insufficient — the assent reflects the 'power and nature' of the agent's mind, its disposition to assent. Brennan then articulates the kind of compatibilism he takes Chrysippus to have held: it is founded on a semantic view about the proper meaning and targets of moral terms (moral praise and blame are praise and blame of people's morals — habits, beliefs, character) and a psychological view of what constitutes a character; external compulsion exculpates, internal causation does not, and the fact that the agent is not the ultimate cause of his character gives no reason to retract a moral assessment of him ('the manager was a lemon, too — but that does not make this a good car').
nodes.label: Brennan: Chrysippus' compatibilism rests on a semantic view of moral terms and a psychological view of character

nodes.description: Brennan's dissent from Bobzien's verdict on Chrysippus (he relies on her reconstruction in Bobzien 1998a but 'diverge[s] from her assessment and verdict', n. 11). The Stoic definition makes P possible iff P is receptive of being true and not hindered from being true by externals. Chrysippus uses it to claim that abstaining was possible for the determined agent, since only his own disposition made him eat. But, Brennan objects, the strategy cheats by moving the dividing-line between 'internal' and 'external': if the first conjunct assesses only the abstract proposition, the agent's psychology falls among the external hindrances and the abstention is impossible; if 'external' means external to the agent's psychology, the psychology resurfaces in the first conjunct. Made explicit, the definition begs the question by systematically excluding psychology. Chrysippus should have conceded that fate makes all events necessary: once one accepts compatibilism about caused actions, it is perverse to strain at necessitarian gnats while swallowing causal camels — the doctrine that fate causes but does not necessitate is an unstable compromise, too much for one side and too little for the other.
nodes.label: Brennan: Chrysippus' definition of possibility equivocates on 'external'; he should have conceded that fate necessitates

nodes.description: Against the usual view that Chrysippus exploded the Lazy Argument (Cicero, De Fato 28-30) as a fallacy by invoking co-fated events, Brennan argues the reply 'crucially failed to understand the original complaint'. First, deliberation: Chrysippus can show that some type of prior event is necessary for a fated outcome, but never that this token action now is necessary (fate could bring recovery about through any number of channels), so desire for the outcome gives no reason to act, and a Newcomb-style analysis makes laziness rational. Second, co-fation merely adds further events not in my control — the rocket-sled thought experiment: crossing the ninety-meter mark is not something the agent does but something done to him. Recast with deliberation's presupposition of openness (an Aristotelian point, De Int. 9; EN III 3), the existence of co-fated events is a common premiss built into the very structure of the Lazy Argument, not a Stoic revelation; the real point of contention is whether deliberation is possible without openness, a challenge there is no evidence the Stoics ever took up. In n. 5 Brennan quotes and criticises Bobzien's probability-based defence of Chrysippus (Bobzien 1998a, 225-226): if inaction is never more futile than action, why not be lazy?
nodes.label: Brennan: the Lazy Argument is powerful and Chrysippus' co-fated reply fails to meet it

nodes.description: Brennan accepts Bobzien's demonstration that the ancient debate over moral responsibility ran on autonomy (the agent, not something external, caused the action) while the modern debate runs on the ability to do otherwise — but holds that 'the contrast between the two conceptions is somewhat obscured in Bobzien's formulation'. People were always interested in both autonomy and the ability to do otherwise; what changed is the conception of the agent with respect to whom the distinctions are drawn. The ancients made autonomy necessary for responsibility precisely because external forces hinder doing otherwise; autonomy mattered because it left the agent free to do otherwise so far as external factors were concerned. The historical evolution is then a shrinking of the self: from the thick ball of beliefs, desires and dispositions (the ancient agent) to a point-like 'ego' or 'will' for which even the agent's own desires count as external hindrances — a conception whose coherence, and compatibility with an explanatory psychology, is doubtful. Searching for a datable moment when the criterion switched would be misguided.
nodes.label: Brennan: the ancient/modern shift in moral responsibility is a shrinking of the self, not a change of criterion

nodes.description: Brennan's account of how the self shrank. Two sources: the Platonic doctrine of the eternal rational soul (Phaedo 66b-d), revived by the Neoplatonists and transmitted to the Church Fathers, Augustine most of all; and a misunderstanding of the Stoic doctrine of assent. Epictetus himself remained orthodox: assent is determined by the agent's overall psychology, and the freedom of assent consists only in the fact that no force external to the psychology can compel or prevent it (Diss. 1.17.21-24; 3.7.15; 1.28.1-7). But Epictetus' talk of 'seeming' is dangerously ambiguous between impression (which comes from outside and is not a desire) and assent (which is the desire); confusing the two yields an un-Stoic impression/desire hybrid the agent can feel yet scrutinize, and a faculty of assent approaching each impression with absolute freedom. Combined with the orthodox identification of the agent with his faculty of assent, the agent comes to seem distinct from his desires, which are reclassified as external — and the self shrinks to a point-like faculty of assent, 'the free and unconstrained will'. Epictetus' own quasi-Platonic language about the body ('you are a little soul, lugging around a corpse', quoted by Brennan at p. 302) abetted the Neoplatonic reading. The modern free-will problem thus traces back to Stoic doctrines, attacks on them, and misunderstandings arising as Stoicism was blended into the Platonic revival underpinning Christian theology.
nodes.label: Brennan: a misreading of Epictetus' doctrine of assent, blended with Platonism, produced the free and unconstrained will

nodes.description: In the Introduction to Determinism and Freedom in Stoic Philosophy, Bobzien expressly brackets the history of the concept of the will from her subject: 'the development of the concept of the will did not spring from the discussion of early Stoic determinism and freedom' — citing the will literature (Gilbert 1963, Voelke 1973, Dihle 1982, Kahn 1988) at n. 27. She does not deny that the early Stoic concept of assent (synkatathesis), and in its wake the Epictetan concept of prohairesis, are essential both for the development of the concept of the will and for the problem of the compatibility of determinism and moral responsibility, and treats them where required (sections 6.3.3-6 and 8.7); but she does not intend to be comprehensive on the matter. The claim demarcates her project from studies, such as Voelke's, that read the Stoic theory of action as a doctrine of will.
nodes.label: Bobzien: the concept of the will did not develop out of the early Stoic determinism-and-freedom discussion

nodes.description: The mise en scène of an ancient opposition between 'necessitarists' (Democritus, Heraclitus, Empedocles, Aristotle) and 'antifatalists', with Chrysippus intervening as an officious arbiter, is doubly implausible: the first three never made fate a philosophical theme (their enrolment converts materialist physics into the terms of a much later debate), Aristotle's presence among necessitarists is contradicted by De Interpretatione 9, Metaphysics E 3 and EN III 1-3 (Ioppolo calls the mention erroneous; Karsten proposed reading Anaxagoras), and the debate's central concept, assent, was introduced only by Zeno. The concordist perspective of §§ 39-45 erases chronology: doctrinal oppositions dissolve into divergent formulations of the same thing, and § 38 gives the last word to 'reason itself'. The veteres category is a value marker of philosophical identity, not a periodization tool. Koch's retained scenario: § 40 presents a new Carneadean objection in continuity with the preceding chapters; § 41 reports a Chrysippean causal distinction not formulated as a response; its reuse as Chrysippus' 'reply' to Carneades (sic occurrit, § 41) is Cicero's own concordist paraphrase.
nodes.label: Koch: the De fato 39 debate among veteres is an anachronistic Ciceronian staging, not a historical dispute

nodes.description: Against the habit of reading the §§ 39-45 argumentative unit (anonymous objection + cylinder reply) in isolation, Koch shows that the earlier chapters prepare it. Cicero's own critique of sympathy (De fato 5-11) already distinguishes 'natural and antecedent' causes of dispositions from the 'principal' causes of particular actions, an Academic-inspired solution analogous to the Chrysippean one; and the objection's unargued postulate — that what arrives by an antecedent cause does not depend on us — rests on Carneades' identification of antecedent with EXTERNAL cause (§§ 23-25, resolving the ambiguity of fieri sine causa), combined with the Aristotelian analysis of constraint as an external principle to which the agent contributes nothing (EN III 1, 1110b1-3; EE II 8). Koch notes that Bobzien herself states the methodological principle of reading the testimony in its totality, but in practice confines the relevant context to §§ 39-45 (p. 373 n. 23).
nodes.label: Koch: De fato 39-45 must be read in continuity with chapters 1-38, whose causal distinctions ground the objection

nodes.description: The manuscripts of De fato 40 present the sequence impulse-then-assent. Koch reviews and rejects the main defences of the transmitted text: Yon's linguistic argument (adpetitus as tendency) cancels itself because Hamelin's correction turns a singular into a plural, the form devoted to acts of impulsion; Inwood's reading through the propatheiai imports a doctrine foreign to the De fato and probably not Chrysippan; Bobzien's hypothesis that adpetitus renders phantasia hormētikē faces two difficulties — the sole surviving testimony (Stobaeus, SVF III 169) defines it as 'what moves impulse' and expressly distinguishes it from impulse, and the term would change sense between objection and reply; Ioppolo's view that the objection targets a pre-Chrysippean (Zenonian) sequence fails because the implication fato fieri = causa antecedente fieri on which the whole argument is built is specifically Chrysippean. The reconstructed ten-step argument is more coherent in the corrected version, and the correction has a decisive advantage neither Hamelin nor Weidemann noted: it gives adpetitus the same 'orthodox' sense in the § 40 objection as it manifestly has in Chrysippus' § 41 reply — without it, Cicero's testimony is incoherent. Against Sharples 1991, who kept the manuscripts.
nodes.label: Koch: Hamelin's correction adpetitus should be adopted — the objection runs on the orthodox assent-then-impulse sequence

nodes.description: The § 41 distinction between causae perfectae et principales and causae adiuvantes et proximae is not so much a conceptual innovation as a redistribution — and thereby a new use — of concepts already present in the De fato's earlier debates: its aim is not to reshape the definition of fate but to find within it something that escapes necessitarianism, leaving the axiom 'everything arrives by an antecedent cause' untouched. Greek correspondences: perfecta = aition autoteles (Plutarch, De stoic. rep. 47, 1056B-D), better rendered 'cause complète' than 'parfaite' (against M. Frede and Long-Sedley) by parallel with the lekton autoteles; proxima = prokatarktikon (with Frede, against Hamelin's and Hankinson's prosechē, which Galen assimilates to synectic causes); principalis = proēgoumenos (Hamelin's suggestion, the most convincing); antecedens = prokatabeblēmenai aitiai (Hamelin, via Alexander's vocabulary); necessaria (§ 44) = 'nécessitante'. The exteriority of the proximate cause, far from indicating constraint as Epicurus and Carneades think, signals its insufficiency to produce the effect by itself.
nodes.label: Koch: Chrysippus' distinction of causes is a redistribution of concepts already in the debate, with precise Greek equivalents

nodes.description: Two readings of the 'nature' that causes assent completely and principally: generic (the rational soul of every human, grounding a general power of saying yes or no — which would make Chrysippus indeterminist) or individual (the actual tension of one's pneuma, by which one person differs from another as cylinder differs from cone within inanimate solids). The analogy's own presupposition — one identical push followed here by rolling, there by turning — supports the individual reading: facing a given representation, being what I am, I am determined by my individual nature to respond favourably or not, with or without reserve, firmly or weakly. The power of acting otherwise is distributed BETWEEN individuals (their psychological and moral diversity), not possessed by a single agent: to free impulse from the external causality of the representation, Chrysippus needs only to reduce the latter to a non-necessitating causality, not to elevate assent into a self-moving power of responding in multiple, in themselves undetermined, ways. Assent and impulse depend on us because they are ours and express what we are — not because we could, the situation being identical, produce other effects.
nodes.label: Koch: the complete cause of assent is the individual pneumatic nature of each hegemonikon — a determinist Chrysippus

metadata.verified_reference: Koch 2011, 438-439 and 447-449 (Vrin, Textes et Traditions 22)

nodes.description: Cicero holds that Chrysippus 'approaches' the antifatalist thesis and finally says the same thing in other words (alia ratio reduced to alia locutio, § 44), because he takes the Chrysippean causal distinction, applied to representation and assent, to found an indetermination of imputable action: the power to make things arrive 'otherwise' (ut aliter eveniant, § 45). This reads assent as a self-moving power on the model Carneades opposed to Epicurus — an interpretation 'qui rend un son bien peu stoïcien'. From Chrysippus' own point of view the antifatalists are wrong: since the proximate cause is not a sufficient cause of assent, one must NOT conclude that assent occurs sine ullo fato (§ 42); his parti-pris is compatibilist, not exceptionalist. Aulus Gellius' parallel summary (NA VII 2), which explains the cylinder as the necessary connection between each temperament and its practical response — with no power of acting otherwise for any single individual — is therefore closer to Chrysippus' doctrine than Cicero's account; the tendency to pull the causal distinction toward indeterminism is entirely absent from it. Koch converges with Vegetti (1991) on this point, and suggests Cicero's interpretive choice even explains his confused presentation of the analogy (and, if one accepts Bobzien's correction, his mistranslation substituting adsensio for mens, p. 444 n. 152).
nodes.label: Koch: Cicero's concordist reading of Chrysippus is already indeterminist; Gellius is closer to the doctrine

nodes.description: Koch declines to make the free-will-problem questionnaire her own frame for reading Alexander. Three reservations: (1) the battery of categories (compatibilism, incompatibilism, non-predeterminism, soft and hard determinism, libertarianism...) insidiously fixes reflection on a game of localisation — placing each author in the right box and endlessly refining new boxes; (2) once a criterion is publicly recognised as pertinent (e.g. categorical vs hypothetical possibility in Alexander's 'power to do otherwise'), commentators read texts like a physician scrutinising a patient for THE symptom, amid a rather confused clinical picture; (3) the sophisticated terminology of contemporary debates creates the illusion of a philosophically mature age entitled to put order into ancient exchanges whose participants lacked full awareness of their own positions — whereas ancient thinkers deprived of our 'lunettes' did not necessarily fail to discern their own stakes. Recourse to modern categories must remain limited, instrumental, and never a finality: reading the De fato is not about establishing whether Alexander already, almost, not quite, or not at all defended an indeterminist conception of human causality. She also objects to Bobzien's methodological declaration (1998a: 137) that textual evidence should decide, since the detection of textual evidence is itself riddled with problems that risk making things undecidable.
nodes.label: Koch: three reservations against reading the De fato through the modern free-will-problem grid

nodes.description: Stoic determinism is indubitably the De fato's principal target, but Alexander names no contemporary: Zeno and Cleanthes never appear in the corpus, Chrysippus nine times, and the usual formula is hoi apo tēs Stoas. Since the difficulties of the Stoic doctrine of fate were debated for five centuries, his interlocutors are most probably imperial-era authors defending a Chrysippan orthodoxy — Theiler and Bobzien identify behind chapters 13-14 (circumstances + proper nature determining necessarily, absent obstacle) a later Stoic theory, possibly Philopator's. This hypothesis grounds a richer alternative to reading the De fato's doctrinal peculiarities as Alexander's clumsy or malicious distortions: after five centuries of inter-school competition, school formulations had simply evolved. The polemic may also fold in other adversaries: Megarians rather than Stoics in chapter 9 (Donini), contemporary Middle Platonist critics such as Galen or Atticus, echoes of intra-Peripatetic debate (Rashed: the internal discussion of the Peripatos as Alexander's most important combat), and possibly school-fictions constructed by Alexander himself from aporiai of the Aristotelian position (Donini, Sharples).
nodes.label: Koch: Alexander's anonymous Stoics are plausibly imperial-era Chrysippan loyalists — evolution, not just distortion

metadata.verified_reference: Koch, La Causalité humaine (Classiques Garnier, 2019), introduction, p. 10-15 (pagination of the on-disk draft)

nodes.description: Against Bobzien 1998: 351-357 (the analogy preserved by Hippolytus is a later contribution reflecting Epictetus, not early Stoic thought, and does not concern compatibilism) and Brennan's endorsement of that verdict, Sharples argues that the analogy can be interpreted in accord with the oldest Stoa. He agrees with Bobzien that it concerns neither the truth of determinism nor its compatibility with responsibility — for any specific dog it is predetermined whether it will follow or resist — but not that it is irrelevant to Stoic freedom: Epictetus' contrast between what is and is not in our power is itself an exact exposition of the school's founding ethical thesis that only virtue is good (playing well IS winning), and the analogy is a good illustration of the doctrine of 'reserve' (hupexairesis; Seneca, De ben. 4.34; Stobaeus, SVF III 564), already presupposed by Chrysippus himself in the passage Bobzien does not discuss, Epictetus Diss. 2.6.9-10 (SVF III 191: follow what is best adapted to nature as long as what follows is unclear), which Inwood had linked to the dog and cart. Accepting the inevitable once it has happened is not fatalism. Philological coda: the 'dragging' motif shared by Seneca's rendering of Cleanthes' prayer (Ep. 107.11, ducunt volentem fata, nolentem trahunt) and the Hippolytus analogy, absent from the prayer as Epictetus quotes it (Man. 53), suggests the analogy may be older than Seneca — perhaps even third-century BCE. Sharples also thinks Bobzien may seriously underestimate the influence of categorical alternative-possibility notions from Aristotle (EN 3.5), Epicurus' swerve and Carneades (Cic. De fato 23-25) onwards, and endorses Brennan's contrast between freedom from external constraint and freedom also from internal psychological constraint, with its link to the shrinking of personal identity via Plato's Phaedo.
nodes.label: Sharples: the dog-and-cart analogy fits early Stoicism as an illustration of the doctrine of reserve — against Bobzien

nodes.description: Reconstruction of the place of divination in Stoic treatises On fate: Ps.-Plutarch De fato 11, 574E-F preserves the headings of (probably) book I of Chrysippus' On fate — two doctrinal points (nothing without a cause, everything by antecedent causes; the world governed by nature, sympnoun and sympathes) followed by three arguments: divination, the acquiescence of the wise, bivalence. Against Bobzien's reconstruction of the divination argument as a first indemonstrable with the Diogenianus sentence as mere justification (Bobzien 1998: 89-90), Gourinat argues that the gar more probably introduces the quotation itself, giving a second indemonstrable ('if everything were not embraced by fate, the predictions of the soothsayers would not be true; but they are true; therefore...'), though the two solutions are logically equivalent. Diogenianus' charge of circular reasoning fails: no source attests that Chrysippus proved divination through fate — divination was established inductively in On divination, and the reciprocity of the gods/divination arguments (Cic. Div. I 10) was spared fallacy because each premiss had independent proof. The sympathy argument is attributable to Chrysippus himself, not only Posidonius: Cicero ascribes it to him at De fato 7, and the Sextus passage (AM IX 79) proving the world a unified body is Chrysippean in doctrine and argument.
nodes.label: Gourinat: divination is Chrysippus' proof of fate; the argument is a second indemonstrable, not circular

metadata.verified_reference: J.-B. Gourinat, « Prediction of the future and co-fatedness », in Natali & Maso (eds.), La catena delle cause (Amsterdam: Hakkert, 2005), 217-232

nodes.description: Diogenianus' dilemma: if divination is useful (announcing what can be avoided), not everything is fated; if everything is fated, divination is useless. The Stoic solution rests on co-fatedness: the precaution-taking actions, and the predictions themselves, are co-fated with the outcomes; Seneca (NQ II 38, 1-4) applies exactly this to expiations — the haruspex is fati minister — and the (presumably Stoic, in most respects Chrysippean) exegesis of Apollo's oracle to Laius in Alexander, De fato 31 makes prophecy itself a means of fate: Apollo, 'author of the things he predicts', knew Laius would disobey, and without the oracle none of the tragic reversal could have occurred (seven textual convergences with Chrysippus are listed). But co-fatedness does not really preserve human responsibility in our sense: it preserves eagerness to act, morality's targets, and the independence of action from EXTERNAL fate, while our actions remain determined; since impulse requires assent (Plut. St. rep. 1057A) and actions are co-fated, assents must be determined too. Conclusion: a completely determinist view of the Stoic system, the only one compatible with everlasting recurrence (Origen, C. Cels. V 20); prediction is useful as one of the means by which providence realises its plans, not as a chance to escape fate. In n. 93 (p. 237) Gourinat expressly withdraws his own earlier position (Gourinat 1996: 118-19) and declares himself no longer confident in Bobzien's assumption (1998: 295) that 'our minds' nature is the result of our acts of assent'.
nodes.label: Gourinat: co-fatedness solves Diogenianus' dilemma but yields a completely determinist Stoicism — assents included

nodes.description: The subject of inquit at De fato 26 ('events that lack causes for their occurrence cannot be true in the future') has always been misread as Chrysippus — so the translations of Yon, Bayer, Sharples 1991 and Barabino, and Bobzien 1998: 8 n. 20 and 68. But the structure of the passage puts the attribution beyond doubt: §§ 26-28 directly follow Carneades' critique of the Epicureans and close with a direct address to them ('your school accepts neither alternative'); nothing marks a transition to the Stoics. On Cicero's testimony it was therefore Epicurus, at the beginning of the Hellenistic age, who introduced the crucial principle that future truth depends on pre-existing causes — inferring, contrapositively to Chrysippus, from the non-existence of fate to the denial of bivalence. Sedley notes that this re-attribution actually reinforces Bobzien's thesis (1998: 75-81) that the Chrysippean nexus between future truth and causes was not shared in the Epicurean testimonia's premisses.
nodes.label: Sedley: the 'inquit' of Cicero De fato 26 is Epicurus, not Chrysippus — Epicurus introduced the truth-causes nexus

metadata.verified_reference: D. Sedley, « Verità futura e causalità nel De fato di Cicerone », in Natali & Maso (eds.), La catena delle cause (Amsterdam: Hakkert, 2005), 247-249

nodes.description: Aristotle's De Interpretatione 9 was unknown to the Hellenistic debate attested in Cicero's De fato: Cicero derides the denial of bivalence as 'miserevole imperizia logica' (Fat. 37-38) — inconceivable had he known Aristotle's chapter — and even lists Aristotle among the 'ancient' determinists (Fat. 39); the debate's eminent logician is instead Diodorus Cronus. The direct Aristotelian inference (antecedent truth → necessity → determinism) is absent: the only argument in play runs 'if already true, it already has causes; if it already has causes, it is predetermined' (a nine-step reconstruction of Chrysippus' bivalence argument, Fat. 20-21, is given). Carneades/Cicero disarm necessity by interpreting it, in Diodorean fashion, as the innocuous immutability of future truth (Fat. 17-18, 28) — a mere fact of the logic of tenses that neither implies antecedent causes nor threatens autonomy — while the real danger lies only in eternal causal chains. Since justifying the Aristotelian intuition now required interposing causality between truth and predetermination, that original intuition generated, for the first time, the concept of a comprehensive causal nexus: 'nacque in questo modo il determinismo'.
nodes.label: Sedley: the Hellenistic fate debate ran through causes, not Aristotelian logical necessity — and so invented determinism

metadata.verified_reference: D. Sedley, « Verità futura e causalità nel De fato di Cicerone », in Natali & Maso (eds.), La catena delle cause (Amsterdam: Hakkert, 2005), 244-257

nodes.description: Cicero was close to the Epicurean milieu from youth — his first teacher was the Epicurean Phaedrus (before 90 BCE, on Maso's re-dating of ad fam. 13.1.2), and 'omnes mihi Epicuri sententiae satis notae sunt' (fin. 1.16) — so his anti-Epicureanism stems neither from ignorance nor misunderstanding. In rendering the swerve, however, Cicero systematically omits the element that saves it from contradiction: where Lucretius (DRN 2.217-220, 259-260) distinguishes the fall, the deviation, and the indeterminable but real moment/place at which deviation OCCURS (incerto tempore ferme incertisque locis — occasionality, the time factor), Cicero's atom 'cum pondere et gravitate directo deorsus feratur, declinare paululum' (nat. d. 1.69) deviates perpetually, as if on a curved path — an explicitly contradictory picture. The De fato 22 'third motion' (declination by an intervallum minimum, elachiston) is equally specious: elachiston in Epicurus refers to a corpusculum, not a deviation, and the plaga is a consequence of the clinamen, not a cause. All four reconstructible Ciceronian configurations of the doctrine come out absurd — which is the point: a programmatic devaluation of Epicureanism by an author who possessed the instruments to understand it, and whose preferred alternative is the animi motus voluntarius Carneades had suggested (fat. 23). Carneades himself, unable to conceive the occasionality of deviation as belonging to the atom's nature, shares the root of the interpretive fallacy.
nodes.label: Maso: Cicero's clinamen suppresses Lucretius' time factor — a deliberate distortion by a connoisseur of Epicureanism

metadata.verified_reference: S. Maso, « Clinamen ciceroniano », in Natali & Maso (eds.), La catena delle cause (Amsterdam: Hakkert, 2005), 258-271

nodes.description: De mixtione 12, 227.1-10 — reducing the major Stoic doctrines (mixture, soul, fate, providence, principles and god, unity and sympathy of the universe) to the 'stupefying' thesis of body passing through body — reads as an agenda of Alexander's anti-Stoic treatises (De mixtione, De anima, De fato, De providentia, De principiis). His antideterminism also reacts against the totalising astrological fatalism of Severan culture, while making real concessions to astral influence, grounded in an enlarged Aristotelian physics of celestial-sublunary interaction; fate is defined complementarily to to eph' hēmin and identified with individual nature (as providence is with cosmic nature) — a concept, physis, central to the treatises but not to the commentaries. The De fato is atypical: an occasional, exoteric gift to the emperors (unique autobiographical notice of the appointment to the Peripatetic chair), defending the koinē prolēpsis that fate exists because universal human agreement is nature speaking. The commentaries, by contrast, never mention Stoic determinism or the body-through-body thesis — one datum among several (statistical style markers, multiple-solution technique) supporting Fazzo's provisional 'dualist' hypothesis on the corpus: the polemical treatises belong to 'Alexander the younger' (the Titus Aurelius Alexander of the recent Aphrodisias epigraph), the core of the commentaries to the earlier exegetical tradition, perhaps his homonymous father.
nodes.label: Fazzo: Alexander's antideterminism belongs to an anti-Stoic treatise programme and a Severan astrological context

metadata.verified_reference: S. Fazzo, « Aristotelismo e antideterminismo... di Alessandro di Afrodisia », in Natali & Maso (eds.), La catena delle cause (Amsterdam: Hakkert, 2005), 272-298

nodes.description: Book XXV of On Nature, occasioned by the theory of psychological development, argues against Democritean mechanism to secure the physical conditions of Epicurus' ethico-pedagogical project. His solution distinguishes the causal contributions of nature, environment and ourselves, and locates a principle of self-determination in the mind's interpretative activity: the developed 'product' (apogegennēmenon), differing from its constituent atoms, acquires emergent, autonomous causal power capable of conditioning their behaviour; from a certain point the subject can correct the orientation of its psychic development by limiting the environment's impact on its constitution. Masi re-reads the famous 'seeds' passage (reading estin for the editors' hēmin) as describing three fundamental developmental tendencies grounded in different material constitutions — matching Seneca's report (Ep. 52.3-6) of Epicurus' three types of men — rather than an absolutely undetermined character at birth. But the treatment is partial: Epicurus never thematises the concatenation of motions transmitted from atoms to aggregate, so he ends by granting dianoia an autonomous causal power without fully justifying it physically. The fuller version of the study is announced as 'Libertà senza clinamen' (Cronache Ercolanesi 36, 2006): the extant book XXV secures freedom without any appeal to the swerve.
nodes.label: Masi: in Peri physeos XXV Epicurus confronts determinism only partially — self-determination without clinamen
